faq.q: When is the best time to see jaguars in the Pantanal?
faq.a: The dry season, roughly June–October, is the whole game: falling water concentrates wildlife on the riverbanks, and late July through early October is the optimum, with August–September the strongest months — Porto Jofre boat-safari sightings run 80–90% over a multi-day trip.

faq.q: Can you self-drive the Transpantaneira?
faq.a: Yes, but it's higher-risk and guided is strongly preferred: a 4x4 is recommended for the 122 wooden bridges, you must fill fuel in Poconé because there are no stations after it, and with no services or cell coverage you must plan the medevac gap yourself.

faq.q: Is the Pantanal good for birding?
faq.a: Exceptionally, and year-round: the wetland lists 650+ bird species, with jabiru storks nesting July–early November and the biggest wading-bird flocks gathering late July to mid-August — a birding counterweight that props up the shoulders of the jaguar season.

faq.q: Can the Pantanal work for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes, as a wild-honeymoon rather than a beach one: SouthWild's Jaguar Suites are 30 m² glass-walled floating rooms with AC and WiFi anchored in the jaguar zone, boats leaving from the deck — private guiding and sundowners over the wetland for the couple who wants adventure over sand.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in the Pantanal?
faq.a: Wildfire in the late dry season: 2020 fires burned about 31% of the wetland and affected roughly 45% of the jaguar population, and 2024 brought the worst fire count since records began in 1999 — well over a million hectares. Monitor fire and air-quality conditions for late-dry departures and keep flexible-rebooking language in the flow.

faq.q: Do I need vaccinations or malaria pills for the Pantanal?
faq.a: It's zone-dependent: CDC notes malaria risk in parts of the state of Mato Grosso (Northern Pantanal) but not in Cuiabá city or Mato Grosso do Sul (Southern Pantanal), so route the health note by access door; yellow-fever vaccination is recommended for Mato Grosso, and dengue/chikungunya precautions apply regardless of malaria zone.

key_facts: The South Coast is a desert-and-ocean circuit ~3–4 hr south of Lima on the Panamericana Sur — no altitude, no cloud-forest; the risks are activity/operator, not crime.
Ballestas Islands ('poor man's Galápagos') — sea lions, Humboldt penguins, boobies, 150+ bird species — visitable only by ~2-hr guided boat from El Chaco pier.

Nazca Lines are best seen on a ~30–35 min light-aircraft overflight from María Reiche Neuman aerodrome (NZC) — choose a reputable operator (accident history; 2022 fatal crash) and expect banking-turn motion sickness.
Huacachina is a real palm-ringed desert oasis outside Ica; the marquee is the sunset dune-buggy + sandboard circuit — ride only permitted buggies (four-point belts + roll cages).
Paracas National Reserve (~S/11 entry) has Playa Roja (Red Beach) and La Catedral; swimming is prohibited at Playa Roja (open swell, strong currents, no lifeguards).

faq.q: Can you swim at the Paracas beaches?
faq.a: Not at the reserve beaches. Playa Roja and the reserve coast have open swell, strong currents and no lifeguards — swimming is prohibited at Playa Roja, and the cliffs at La Catedral are crumbly and railing-less. Safe bay swimming is at the resort waterfronts, not inside the reserve (~S/11 entry).

faq.q: How old are the Nazca Lines, and what will I see?
faq.a: They date to the Nazca culture ~300–600 AD. From a ~30–35 min overflight you'll pick out the hummingbird, monkey, spider and condor cut into the desert at a scale invisible from the ground; a roadside mirador shows 2–3 figures for those who'd rather not fly.

faq.q: What's the Ica Vendimia and pisco scene?
faq.a: Ica is the cradle of Peruvian pisco and wine. Historic bodegas — Tacama, Vista Alegre, El Catador, Ocucaje, Queirolo/Intipalka — run tastings year-round, peaking at the March Vendimia grape-harvest festival with 40+ activities, grape-treading and tastings across the city.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: Activity safety and operator choice, not crime. The load-bearing calls are the Nazca light-aircraft overflight (authorized operators only; 2022 fatal crash), the Huacachina dune-buggy (rollover risk), Ballestas boat life-vests and Pacific riptides. High winds/dust and winter garúa can also suspend flights.

faq.q: Is the Huacachina dune buggy dangerous?
faq.a: It carries real rollover risk on the steep dunes, so operator choice matters. Peru's minimum standard requires four-point seatbelts, roll cages, headrests, certified welds and a 15-year max vehicle age; the transport ministry has warned against informal "tubular" buggies. Ride only permitted operators and check your belts.

faq.q: What is Petra?
faq.a: A 2,000-year-old Nabataean city carved into rose-red sandstone - the Siq gorge, the Treasury (Al-Khazneh), the Monastery, and Petra by Night by candlelight. UNESCO World Heritage since 1985 and one of the New7Wonders of the World.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Petra?
faq.a: March-April and October-November - clear light on the sandstone and comfortable days. Summer reaches about 40C (tour early morning); winter is cold with rain and occasional snow.

faq.q: What does the Jordan Pass cover?
faq.a: It bundles Petra entry (1-3 days by tier), 40+ sites including Wadi Rum entry and Jerash, and waives the tourist-visa fee if you stay at least 3 nights. Buy it online before arrival. It does not cover Petra by Night, jeep tours or overnight camps - those are separate bookings.

name: Placencia
line: Whale sharks and mainland sand

key_facts: Placencia is Belize's southern beach peninsula with the country's best mainland beaches and its main resort/romance-wedding coast.
Gladden Spit, off Placencia, is the world's most predictable whale-shark aggregation, timed to the Mar-Jun full moons (peak Apr-May).
The southern barrier reef (Silk Cayes, Laughing Bird Caye NP, South Water Caye) launches from Placencia; the outer atolls are reachable.
Monkey River (howler monkeys, manatees) and the Cockscomb Basin (world's first jaguar preserve) are easy day trips.
Access is BZE -> PLJ (Placencia airstrip) by 20-30 min puddle-jumper on Tropic Air / Maya Island Air; ~3.5-4 hr drive alternative.

faq.q: Is Placencia good for a honeymoon or wedding?
faq.a: Yes — it is Belize's most credible mainland resort/romance market, with real luxury-to-ultra range. Naïa Resort & Spa (39 beach houses + treetop villas on 224 private acres, mile of beach, from ~US$380/night) and SLH-member Itz'ana anchor the beachfront, plus true private-island elopements offshore. The peninsula earns both the wedding and the dive log.

faq.q: When can you swim with whale sharks in Placencia?
faq.a: Around the Mar–Jun full moons at Gladden Spit — the one place on the planet where whale-shark arrival is "reasonably predictable." 2026 full moons are Mar 14, Apr 13, May 12 and Jun 11, with windows ~2 days before to ~10 days after; April and May fill first, so serious divers book three to four months ahead. Encounters are not guaranteed — you're buying the window.

faq.q: What wildlife can you see near Placencia?
faq.a: Two flagship day trips. The Monkey River eco-tour (a ~45-min coastal boat run then a river cruise) carries you into black-howler-monkey habitat with crocodiles, iguanas, toucans and manatees on the return; and the Cockscomb Basin — the world's first jaguar preserve, 128,000 acres, est. 1986 — is a half-day inland via Maya Center.

faq.q: Does Placencia have good beaches and reef?
faq.a: Yes — the country's best mainland beaches on a 16-mile peninsula, plus the closest mainland launch to the southern reef. Splash Dive Center's home waters — the Silk Cayes, South Water Caye and Laughing Bird Caye — are "postcard perfect islands on the barrier reef" with turtles, sharks, rays and eels, most a 30–60 minute run out.

faq.q: Can you fly-fish the flats in Placencia?
faq.a: Yes — the southern flats and river mouths are world-class permit water, fishable year-round for permit, bonefish and tarpon by skiff. It's a high-value niche booked through Placencia fishing lodges and guides, and a reliable green-season lever when the reef days are between fronts.

faq.q: Is there a destination spa / wellness stay in Placencia?
faq.a: Yes — Naïa Resort & Spa is built for it: a 224-acre private property with a mile of beach, a destination spa and a private-island couples retreat, strong on both romance and wellness. It's the anchor for a quiet-beach reset paired with reef or river days.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Placencia?
faq.a: Dive-chamber distance and open-water boat runs, not crime. The nearest recompression chamber is on Ambergris Caye (San Pedro), a meaningful distance north of the southern reef, so plan conservative profiles and no-fly windows; the run to Gladden Spit is ~90 minutes each way with early 6–7am departures. There is no full trauma center on the peninsula — serious cases evacuate to Belize City.

faq.q: Is swimming with whale sharks dangerous?
faq.a: It runs guided-only with a permitted operator — Gladden Spit is inside a marine reserve and only permitted operators may run the aggregation, no-touch and no-chase. Snorkelers work the surface aggregation over 2–3 hours (moderate swimming ability needed); divers descend to ~50–80 ft to meet the sharks and must be certified and guided.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Playa del Carmen?
faq.a: Sargassum, weather and water — not violent crime against tourists. 2026 is a record-forecast sargassum year, but Playa is moderate risk thanks to active municipal cleanup and a 5-km double-barrier program, with landings in pulses. Drink bottled water, use repellent for dengue (peak May–Nov, no malaria), and note hurricane season runs June–November.

faq.q: Can I dive Cozumel and the cenotes from Playa del Carmen?
faq.a: Yes — Playa is the best mainland dive base for both. Cozumel's drift-wall reef (Palancar, Santa Rosa, Columbia) is a 40-minute ferry away at ~US$32 round trip, and cenote cavern dives sit under 30 minutes inland. Cozumel walls are drift dives for a reputable operator; cenotes are guide-required and weather-independent.

faq.q: What is there to do on Fifth Avenue?
faq.a: Fifth Avenue (Quinta Avenida) is the Riviera Maya's densest dining and nightlife strip — a multi-kilometre pedestrian street of tacos-to-rooftop bars parallel to the sand. It is the town's social spine, best on a weekday evening before the crowds; guided food-and-rooftop crawls are the easy way to graze it.

faq.q: Are the Xcaret and Xplor parks worth it, especially for families?
faq.a: Yes — they are the region's marquee eco-parks. Xcaret runs cenotes, underground rivers and Maya performances; Xplor has Mexico's largest zipline circuit (14 lines over 3.8 km) plus amphibious buggies. Park admission (~US$85–110 at Xcaret) is pass-through, and both sit just outside town — a full family day out.

faq.q: Can I visit Maya ruins from Playa del Carmen?
faq.a: Yes — it is the corridor's best ruins base. Tulum's cliff-top ruins and Cobá's bikeable jungle pyramids pair in one day loop, and Chichén Itzá is a longer day trip; early morning (Nov/Feb) is best. Amstar and other DMCs run guided excursions, with ruin entry as a pass-through cost.

faq.q: Where's the best luxury for a honeymoon near Playa del Carmen?
faq.a: The Mayakoba estate and La Casa de la Playa. Mayakoba (Rosewood, Banyan Tree, Andaz) is a gated 595-acre lagoon estate of Virtuoso-affiliated flagships; La Casa de la Playa (Grupo Xcaret) is a 63-suite AAA Five-Diamond boutique ranked #1 Resort in Mexico for 2025. Both are ultra-tier honeymoon addresses on Playa's doorstep.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Playa del Carmen?
faq.a: November–March is the dry, cooler high season (best weather, highest rates); May–October is hot, humid and rainy at the cheapest rates. The value sweet spots are the May–June and November shoulders at ~30–40% off, with November landing clear of sargassum and ahead of the holiday surge.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Puerto Aventuras?
faq.a: Water, mosquitoes, hurricanes and sargassum — not crime. Drink bottled/purified water, use repellent for dengue (peak May–November, no malaria in tourist Quintana Roo), and note hurricane season runs June–November. Sargassum is heavy region-wide in 2026 (Apr–Aug), but the marina and dive focus soften the beach hit here.

faq.q: What is the marina and sportfishing like in Puerto Aventuras?
faq.a: It is one of the few mainland deep-water marinas between Cancún and Belize City — a secure safe-haven harbor for yachts, sailors and sportfishers. Offshore charters run year-round (weather permitting), with the peak billfish and mahi window in the Mar–Jun spring dry season; berth fees are pass-through and the guided charter is the commissionable wrapper.

faq.q: Is Puerto Aventuras a good dive base?
faq.a: Yes — it is a genuine near-shore reef and cenote base. The reef is only ~100 feet from the beach, so you can log several dives a day with minimal boat transit, and Cenote Azul (between Puerto Aventuras and Playa del Carmen) puts cave country within easy reach. Best reef visibility runs Nov–May.

faq.q: Is Puerto Aventuras good for families?
faq.a: Very — it is built for calm, safe family days. The adjacent Dolphin Discovery center offers sea-inlet swims with bottlenose dolphins, sea lions and manatees; add the gated 24/7-security layout, a calm marina promenade and near-shore reef, and it suits families and multigenerational groups well.

faq.q: Is Puerto Aventuras good for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes, for couples who want secure and quiet over party energy. The in-community options are the branded all-inclusive Dreams Aventuras and private gated marina/golf villas with chef and concierge; the wider luxury tier runs ~US$400–600+/night in March. For branded ultra, Mayakoba (Rosewood, Banyan Tree) is ~30–40 min north with an easy marina/dive day trip.

faq.q: Can I do Maya ruins from Puerto Aventuras?
faq.a: Yes — Tulum and Cobá are easy guided day trips, alongside Akumal's turtle bay ~10 min south. Amstar and other Riviera Maya DMCs run cenote, Tulum-ruins and Akumal-turtle excursions from Puerto Aventuras; entries are pass-through, with the guided excursion the commissionable wrapper.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Puerto Aventuras?
faq.a: December–April is peak (best weather, highest rates); the value windows are the May–June and November shoulders at ~30–40% off, with November clear of sargassum. The green season (Jun–mid-Oct) is hot, rainy and cheapest with hurricane exposure — but the marina and dive product hold up better than a pure beach stay.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Puerto Morelos?
faq.a: Sargassum, hurricanes and water — not crime. 2026 is heavy region-wide for sargassum, and Puerto Morelos' open Caribbean-facing beaches are affected, so plan cenote and reef days as hedges; drink bottled water, use repellent for dengue (no malaria in the tourist zone), and note hurricane season runs June–November, September riskiest.

faq.q: Is Puerto Morelos good for diving and the Juan Escutia wreck?
faq.a: Yes — it is an underrated day-boat dive base. The Puerto Morelos Reef National Park sits under 500 m offshore, one of the Caribbean's best-preserved reefs, and the sunken Juan Escutia is now an artificial reef and fish refuge steps away. Visibility is best in the dry Oct–March window; book in town, where it is cheaper and supports local operators.

faq.q: Can I go deep-sea fishing from Puerto Morelos?
faq.a: Yes — it is a working fishing port, so charters are authentic and close at hand. Half- and full-day trips target dorado (mahi-mahi), wahoo, tuna and barracuda, with gear and guide included; the species mix is seasonal, so confirm with the operator. It pairs naturally with the fresh-off-the-boat ceviche at the beachfront cantinas.

faq.q: What is the Route of the Cenotes?
faq.a: A ~17 km jungle road of cenotes running inland from town — Puerto Morelos is its northern gateway. It strings together open, semi-open and cave cenotes for swimming, cavern diving and ziplining, at roughly 150–250 MXN entry each. Because they are shaded jungle sites, cenotes are weather-resilient — a strong rainy-day and green-season option.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: Staying in the tourist zone, not the interior. Fly into PVR (no need to transit the restricted interior), remain within PV / the Banderas Bay resort corridor, and don't self-drive into the Jalisco interior. Health-wise, dengue is seasonal in the Jul–Oct rains — use repellent — and there is no malaria in the resort zone.

faq.q: When and how can I see the whales?
faq.a: On a licensed panga, roughly Dec 8–Mar 23, best in the morning. Around 500–700 humpbacks arrive in Banderas Bay each winter to breed and calve within sight of shore; whales are federally protected, so keep the regulated distance and do not swim with them. Morning departures mean calmer seas.

faq.q: Is Puerto Vallarta good for a honeymoon, and where's the top end?
faq.a: Yes — it's a mature honeymoon and destination-wedding market. The in-city ultra rung is narrow but real: Hotel Mousai is PV's only AAA Five-Diamond (145 suites + 4 penthouses), and the 9-room Casa Kimberly is the Taylor/Burton love-story hotel. Peak is Nov–Apr; hold marquee rooms and villas early.

faq.q: Can beginners dive Los Arcos?
faq.a: Los Arcos is a certified-diver site, not a beginner pool — it holds the deepest water in Banderas Bay, with tunnels, arches, rays and turtles. Dive within your certification, and observe the DAN no-fly interval of 18–24 hours before boarding a flight from PVR. Marietas Islands is the other certified-reef option.

faq.q: Where are the best villas?
faq.a: Conchas Chinas and Amapas. PV's "Beverly Hills" hillside enclave holds beachfront estates with private chef and butler just 5–10 minutes from the Romantic Zone; book Dec–Mar (the whale-and-holiday peak) 4–6+ months ahead. Route villas as agency/host merchant-of-record, never net-rate resale.

name: Puerto Viejo (Southern Caribbean)
line: Costa Rica's Southern Caribbean

key_facts: Puerto Viejo de Talamanca is Costa Rica's Southern Caribbean counter-culture coast: Afro-Caribbean + Bribri, reggae-slow beach towns, distinct from the Pacific side.
The Caribbean coast INVERTS the national weather pattern - driest and calmest in Sep-Oct and Feb-Mar, exactly when the Pacific is 'green season' - a counter-seasonal selling point.
Cahuita National Park protects both a coral reef (guided snorkel only, ~$20pp) and a coastal rainforest walk with sloths, monkeys, iguanas and coatis.
Salsa Brava is an expert-only shallow reef break over sharp coral; beginners surf the Playa Cocles beach break; Punta Uva and Manzanillo are the calm swimming beaches.
Access is international via SJO (San Jose), then a ~4-4.5 hr drive southeast via Limon - a real distance, not a short transfer.

safety.hospital: 24-hr private clinic in Puerto Viejo + public clinic Hone Creek (~5km); nearest hospital Limon (~1hr); major trauma routes to San Jose
safety.medical_evacuation: AirMed/Global Rescue-type air ambulance toward San Jose/repatriation; ~US$50,000 often full straight
safety.petty_crime: opportunistic theft is main risk (phones/wallets/purses); don't leave beach valuables unattended, avoid poorly lit streets alone at night, don't resist a robbery
safety.air_access_verified: SJO (San Jose) -> ~4-4.5 hr drive via Limon to Puerto Viejo (distance flag)
safety.riptide: Caribbean riptide risk; Salsa Brava = expert-only reef break over sharp coral; swim at calmer beaches (Punta Uva, Manzanillo)
safety.wildlife: snake/wildlife on jungle & national-park trails - go guided, stay on trail, no-touch
safety.dengue: seasonal mosquito-borne risk, occasional outbreaks; repellent advised
safety.malaria: low/localized; negligible in beach-town zone; relevant only for deep-forest hikes
safety.water: generally potable in Costa Rica incl. most of this zone; sensitive travelers/remote lodges may prefer bottled - confirm at property

faq.q: Do you need a guide to snorkel Cahuita National Park?
faq.a: Yes — Cahuita's reef snorkel is guided-only (~US$20 pp); you can't bring your own gear and go solo, single-use plastics are banned, and no-touch coral discipline applies. Book the guided boat snorkel for best visibility Mar–Apr and Aug–Oct.

faq.q: Is Puerto Viejo good for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes, as barefoot-luxury rather than palace-luxury. The ceiling is premier-to-luxury boutique — Le Cameleon (SLH) from ~US$186/night, or the 7-bungalow Tierra de Sueños wellness hideaway in Playa Chiquita — jungle-beach seclusion, adults-leaning, no marble required.

faq.q: When is Limón Carnival, and can you base in Puerto Viejo for it?
faq.a: Yes. Limón Carnival runs every October (started 1949) in the port city of Limón — soca, calypso, reggae and parades — with Puerto Viejo a common lodging hub a short hop south; confirm exact 2026 dates on live tracking.

faq.q: Can you see sloths and dolphins around Puerto Viejo?
faq.a: Easily. The town is ringed by jungle, so sloths, monkeys and colorful birds show right off the coast road, and the 23,348-acre Gandoca-Manzanillo refuge holds year-round bottlenose and tucuxi dolphins plus four sea-turtle species (Mar–Jul).

faq.q: Can beginners surf Salsa Brava?
faq.a: No. Salsa Brava is an expert-only, powerful, shallow reef break over sharp coral — one of Central America's heaviest waves — and it injures those who fall. Beginners and intermediates belong at the Playa Cocles beach break or a gentler beach; distinguish clearly at point of sale.

faq.q: How far is medical care if something goes wrong?
faq.a: A 24-hour private clinic in Puerto Viejo handles emergencies, with a public clinic in Hone Creek (~5 km) and the nearest large hospital in Limón (~1 hr); major trauma routes to San José. Air-evac cases can run ~US$50,000, often full straight — carry robust travel + air-evac insurance.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Punta Cana?
faq.a: Small stuff, not violent crime: pickpocketing/theft, unlicensed excursion operators, beach rip currents and strong sun. Malaria is low but present in La Altagracia (mosquito precautions), and hurricane season is Jun-Nov (peak Aug-Oct) - carry travel insurance for a green-season trip.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Punta Cana?
faq.a: December-April is the dry, reliable peak (best weather, highest prices); March-May is the sweet spot for thinner crowds and deals; July-October is cheapest but overlaps hurricane season, so watch forecasts.

faq.q: What currency do I need in Punta Cana, and what about entry?
faq.a: The Dominican peso (DOP, ~58/USD) is official, but US dollars are accepted almost everywhere at resorts - carry small DOP for tips. Entry needs a valid passport, no visa (30 days), the $10 tourist card bundled in your airfare, and a mandatory E-Ticket before you fly.

faq.q: Is the Isla Saona day trip worth it?
faq.a: Yes - it's the most popular excursion: a catamaran and speedboat day to a national-park island of shallow natural pools and white sand, with the turtle-conservation village of Mano Juan. It sells out in peak, so book ahead through a licensed operator.

faq.q: Is Punta Cana only all-inclusive resorts, and how many days do I need?
faq.a: The resorts are the core (5-7 nights is typical), but the East rewards getting out: Saona, Hoyo Azul/Scape Park, ATV + Macao horseback, catamaran snorkel and championship golf. Budget a couple of excursion days beyond the beach.

faq.q: Which Punta del Este beach should I swim at — Mansa or Brava?
faq.a: Swim at Playa Mansa. The Mansa (calm Río de la Plata bay side) is gentle and family-friendly for swimming; Playa Brava faces the open Atlantic with strong waves and dangerous currents, best left to surfers and lifeguard-patrolled zones. The La Mano sculpture on Brava was built in 1982 as a literal warning about those currents.

faq.q: Is Punta del Este good for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes — it is a co-primary romance destination. The boho-luxe play is a José Ignacio villa or a Vik suite, a Casapueblo sunset with sparkling wine (the Ceremonia al Sol has played daily since 1994), a fish-on-the-sand dinner at La Huella, and — if timing allows — NYE fireworks on the bay. José Ignacio is quieter and older-money than the peninsula's party core.

faq.q: What's the food-and-wine scene in Punta del Este?
faq.a: It is one of the region's strongest. Parador La Huella grills the day's catch on the José Ignacio sand (routinely on Latin America's 50 Best); inland, Francis Mallmann's Restaurante Garzón does open-fire cooking in a revived near-ghost town, and Bodega Garzón pours award-winning Tannat with a Mallmann-directed fire kitchen.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Punta del Este?
faq.a: The Atlantic surf. Playa Brava's open-Atlantic waves and rip currents are the headline hazard — La Mano is literally the warning sign. Swim only in patrolled zones when lifeguards are on duty, and steer weak swimmers and children to the calm Playa Mansa bay side.

faq.q: Are the Isla de Lobos boat trip and Cabo Polonio dangerous?
faq.a: Not with a sanctioned operator. The ~2-hour Isla de Lobos crossing is open Atlantic — go on an operated launch with life jackets, and note that landing on the reserve is prohibited. Cabo Polonio is off-grid and reachable only by sanctioned 4×4 or horseback across the dunes; you cannot drive your own car in, so use an operator and treat it as a genuine wilderness day.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: Rip currents and dengue, not crime. The Pacific beaches have rip currents and shore break — swim guarded resort beaches and obey the flags — and Nayarit is a high-prevalence dengue state with a May–November transmission peak, so pack repellent for summer stays. Nearest full trauma is Puerto Vallarta (~40 min), then US air-evac.

faq.q: Is Punta Mita good for a destination wedding?
faq.a: It is one of Mexico's ultra-wedding flagships. Susurros del Corazón (Auberge) alone hosts events for 30–300 guests ~45 minutes from PVR, with reception rental from $2,000, alongside Four Seasons and St. Regis event teams. Villa and resort weddings book 9–12 months out — peak-season cohorts 12+ months.

faq.q: What's the best beach and surf for beginners?
faq.a: El Anclote. It's a sheltered, sandy-bottom cove with gentle rolling waves — the peninsula's beginner classroom — while La Lancha, a ~10-minute jungle-trail walk away, holds the most reliable quality waves for confident beginners through intermediates. Guided lessons ($60–180) stage away from the rocks.

faq.q: Is the golf as good as they say?
faq.a: Yes — it's a two-course Nicklaus complex with a genuine one-of-a-kind hole. The Pacífico course (7,104-yd par-72, eight ocean holes) has the "Tail of the Whale," the world's only natural-island green, 199 yards offshore and walkable at low tide; the 2009 Bahía course is the more technical of the two.

faq.q: How do I actually visit the Islas Marietas Hidden Beach?
faq.a: Only with a SEMARNAT-permitted operator, and book weeks ahead. Playa del Amor is capped at ~116 visitors/day, Wed–Sun, reached by a ~15-minute boat then a life-jacketed swim through a low cave tunnel; non-swimmers can't access it. Never promise a landing without a confirmed permitted slot.

faq.q: Where can I go on safari instead, right now?
faq.a: Kenya (Maasai Mara / Amboseli, US L2, bookable) or Tanzania (Serengeti / Ngorongoro, US L3, bookable) for the classic Big-game plains - or Akagera, Rwanda (US L3, a Big-Five comeback ~2h from Kigali) for the nearest live savanna. We route all Uganda safari demand there.

faq.q: Will this clear - should I wait for Queen Elizabeth?
faq.a: Possibly - this is a health-driven, dynamic advisory (an outbreak, not conflict), so it can be lifted when the outbreak is contained. We re-verify Uganda's status every publish cycle and will flip the park to bookable the moment it drops below Level 4. For a firm 2026 safari, book Kenya, Tanzania or Akagera now.

faq.q: What would Queen Elizabeth offer when it reopens?
faq.a: Uganda's most popular savanna - the tree-climbing lions of Ishasha, the Kazinga Channel boat cruise (hippos, crocs, elephants, 600+ birds), Kyambura Gorge chimps, and a Rift-Valley backdrop of crater lakes. All held until the advisory lifts.

faq.q: Is the DRC border a concern too?
faq.a: Yes - separately. The park's western edge borders Virunga in the DR Congo, a standing security concern in its own right; when the park is live, itineraries keep to the eastern/central sectors. But the Ebola L4 is the disqualifying fact today, and it holds the whole park.

faq.q: What are the non-Ebola health requirements for Uganda?
faq.a: Yellow fever is mandatory for entry (all travelers >=1 yr, checked at Entebbe, vaccinate >=10 days before); malaria prophylaxis is essential (all regions); carry AMREF Flying Doctors + insurance. All moot while the L4 hold stands.

faq.q: What exactly is the danger in the Quirimbas?
faq.a: An active ISIS-linked insurgency (ASWJ). Armed groups have attacked villages and occupied islands in the archipelago and the mainland port of Mocimboa da Praia; foreigners have been kidnapped, and the 2021 Palma attack killed or displaced thousands. Marine and health hazards are secondary to the conflict.

faq.q: Could I go with a private security arrangement or a waiver?
faq.a: No - TravelWell offers no waiver and no book path for a Level 4 zone. Evacuation from a remote island in an active-conflict setting is not assured, and even the gateway city of Pemba is high-risk. The responsible answer is to wait for the advisory to change.

faq.q: Is the rest of Mozambique off-limits too?
faq.a: No - this hold is Cabo Delgado-specific. Southern Mozambique (Maputo, Tofo, Vilanculos, the Bazaruto Archipelago, Inhambane) is far from the conflict and remains a bookable Indian-Ocean destination; that is where we point Mozambique demand today.

faq.q: When the advisory clears, what would the Quirimbas offer?
faq.a: Elite diving (Neptune's Arm and untouched reefs), humpback whales and whale sharks in season, the Swahili stone town of Ibo, and barefoot-luxury private islands (Medjumbe, Vamizi) - a world-class dive-and-heritage archipelago. All of it is held until the advisory lifts.

faq.q: What are the non-security health risks to know?
faq.a: Malaria is HIGH (prophylaxis + bite prevention essential), cyclone season is Dec-Apr, yellow-fever proof is needed only if arriving from an endemic country, and in-conflict medical/evacuation capacity is minimal - reinforcing the booking hold.

faq.q: Why is Quito's Old Town so famous?
faq.a: Because it was the first UNESCO World Heritage Site ever inscribed, in 1978 (alongside Kraków), and remains the largest, best-preserved historic center in the Americas. Its jewel is La Compañía de Jesús, whose central nave is almost entirely covered in gold leaf after 160 years of construction (1605–1765); entry is ~$5.

faq.q: What are the best adventure day trips from Quito?
faq.a: Quito is the launchpad for high-altitude Andes adventure. Top picks: Cotopaxi (5,897 m active volcano, 1h45 south), Quilotoa's 250 m-deep turquoise crater lake (~3-hr drive) and Mindo's 500+ bird species two hours northwest, with cloud-forest ziplines, waterfalls and tubing. Volcano climbs are guided-only.

faq.q: Where do couples stay near Quito for a romantic Andes escape?
faq.a: In restored colonial mansions or working-estate haciendas. The 10-room Illa Experience Hotel in the San Marcos creative quarter is an intimate couples' retreat steps from the Old Town sights, while the 17th-century Hacienda Zuleta at ~2,900 m, ~2 hrs north, offers horseback riding and whole-estate buyouts for weddings.

faq.q: Is Quito just a stopover for Galápagos?
faq.a: It is the essential gateway, and worth a night or two in its own right. Quito's Mariscal Sucre (UIO) is the primary air gateway feeding Galápagos and the Amazon, so most Quito nights ride the bigger cruise curve as a pre/post-Galápagos stay; at 2,850 m (9,350 ft) the city also doubles as the acclimatization night before the Andes.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Quito?
faq.a: Altitude, not crime. ~88% of Ecuador's homicides occur in five coastal provinces and Quito's homicide rate runs below many mid-sized US cities; the real headline is that the city sits at 2,850 m (9,350 ft), where mild AMS is common within 24 hours of arrival — arrive, hydrate, go slow on day 1, skip alcohol, and acclimatize before any climb.

faq.q: Is climbing Cotopaxi dangerous?
faq.a: Yes — it is mountaineering, guided-only. Cotopaxi (5,897 m) involves glacier travel, crevasse risk and real HAPE/HACE exposure; it requires a certified mountain guide, a rope team, 2–3 days of prior acclimatization at 3,000–3,500 m, and evacuation insurance. Never freelance it — even Rucu Pichincha (~4,700 m) deposits you at 4,000 m with no acclimatization.

faq.q: What is the current advisory for Raja Ampat, and how do I dive it responsibly?
faq.a: The U.S. State Department places Indonesia at Level 2 - Exercise Increased Caution (reissued 30 April 2025). Its only Level 4 (Do Not Travel) carve-outs are Central Papua (Papua Tengah) and Highland Papua (Papua Pegunungan); Raja Ampat sits in Southwest Papua (Papua Barat Daya), outside both, at the country caution baseline. The UK FCDO issues no formal advise-against level for Papua but notes armed separatist violence mainly in Highland and Central Papua, calls that security picture unpredictable, and says to take local advice; it does not name Raja Ampat. The stricter reading - the State Level 2 baseline plus the broader Papua-context caveat - sets the posture. One live note: Wayag Island and the Manyaifun/Batangpele area were reported temporarily closed to visitors over local nickel-mining disputes, so confirm current access for northern itineraries. Carry DAN membership plus dive-accident insurance with strong evacuation cover, and observe an 18-24 hour no-fly window after diving.

faq.q: Is there a recompression chamber, and how remote is care?
faq.a: The nearest recompression chamber is in Waisai, the regency capital on Waigeo, roughly 2-4 hours from the dive sites. Its readiness cannot be assumed: dive-medicine sources warn there is no reliably operational chamber in Papua, and a DAN-documented case describes the Waisai chamber being under repair with the diver evacuated to Bali - nearly 2,000 km and around seven hours' flying (about four hours to Sorong, three more to Bali); Manado in North Sulawesi is the other referral. Treat Waisai as the nearest option, confirm its status through the operator or DAN, and carry evacuation insurance that will actually move you. Conservative profiles and nitrox matter more here than almost anywhere.

faq.q: When is the best time to dive Raja Ampat?
faq.a: The main liveaboard window is roughly October-April, when seas are calmer and visibility is at its clearest; June-July brings the most unpredictable conditions and is best avoided, and several boats reposition to Komodo for the Southeast-monsoon dry season. Water stays around 28-30C year-round.

faq.q: Where do I see mantas, and what is the marquee dive?
faq.a: Manta Sandy in the Dampier Strait and Magic Mountain (Shadow Reef) in Misool are the two manta cleaning stations - reef mantas through much of the year and oceanic mantas in season at Magic Mountain. The marquee reef dive is Cape Kri, which holds a record for the most fish species logged on a single dive.

faq.q: Dampier Strait, Misool or Wayag - how does a liveaboard week split?
faq.a: Most trips run 7-12 nights to cover the three regions: the Dampier Strait in the centre (Cape Kri, Blue Magic, Sardine Reef, Manta Sandy, Arborek), Misool in the south (Boo Windows, Magic Mountain, Four Kings, Fiabacet) and the Wayag/north karst seascape (Kawe, The Passage). Longer charters reach all three; shorter ones concentrate on Dampier and one wing.

faq.q: What conditions and certification should I plan for?
faq.a: Many of the best sites - Blue Magic, Cape Kri, Sardine Reef - are current-driven drift dives where a reef hook and good buoyancy earn their place; sheltered reefs, jetties (Arborek) and the mangrove channel of The Passage suit a wider range with a guide. Nitrox is standard on liveaboards for the repetitive multi-day profile. Dive within your certification and the operator briefing.

faq.q: How far ahead do Raja Ampat liveaboards book?
faq.a: The October-April peak on preferred vessels fills earliest - the dedicated Raja Ampat vessels and luxury phinisi are booked well ahead; hold roughly 6-12 months out for peak windows and marquee boats, nearer term for the shoulder. Confirm per-vessel lead times with the operator.

faq.q: What is the current advisory for the Egyptian Red Sea, and how do I dive it responsibly?
faq.a: The U.S. State Department places Egypt at Level 2 - Exercise Increased Caution (accessed 2026-08-09). The Northern and Middle Sinai Peninsula and parts of the Western Desert carry a Level 4 (Do Not Travel) carve-out; the Red Sea coast sits outside every carve-out, so Hurghada and the northern Red Sea coast carry no sub-zone restriction. The UK FCDO draws the same interior zones in its own words and names no Red Sea resort; the stricter baseline (State Level 2) sets the posture. Carry DAN membership plus separate dive-accident insurance and observe an 18-24 hour no-fly window after diving.

faq.q: Is there a recompression chamber, and how remote is care?
faq.a: The Red Sea coast runs a dense chamber network. Northern routes are covered by the Hyperbaric Medical Center in Sharm el-Sheikh (DAN Egypt) and HyperMed in Hurghada (next to the airport); southern routes by Baro Medical in Marsa Shagra (about 20 km north of Marsa Alam) and the DECO International chamber in Hamata (a 24-hour recompression and medical-emergency facility about 135 km south of Marsa Alam). Confirm the chamber covering your itinerary and its readiness on your dates via the operator or DAN. Offshore reefs are hours from port, so insurance and a conservative profile matter most there.

faq.q: When is the best time to dive the Red Sea?
faq.a: March-May and September-November are the optimal windows - calm seas, warm water and 30 m+ visibility. Summer (June-August) pushes water to 30C with strong offshore shark action but occasional plankton; winter (December-February) drops to 21-23C and can be windy offshore.

faq.q: When can I see oceanic whitetips, hammerheads and threshers?
faq.a: June-November is the offshore shark window: oceanic whitetips, grey reef and scalloped hammerheads around Daedalus and Elphinstone, with The Brothers known for thresher sharks in the early morning.

faq.q: North route or south route - which liveaboard week?
faq.a: North runs the wrecks and reefs - SS Thistlegorm, Abu Nuhas, Ras Mohammed and the Straits of Tiran (Jackson, Woodhouse, Thomas, Gordon). South runs the offshore shark reefs (Brothers, Daedalus, Elphinstone) and the remote Fury Shoals and St John's near the Sudan border; liveaboards favour the calm southern conditions in summer.

faq.q: What certification and conditions should I plan for?
faq.a: The offshore reefs (Brothers, Daedalus, Elphinstone) are current-swept blue-water sites suited to experienced divers; the northern wrecks and Tiran reefs suit a wider range with a guide. Nitrox is standard on most liveaboards for the repetitive multi-day profile. Dive within your certification and the operator briefing.

faq.q: How far ahead do Red Sea liveaboards book?
faq.a: Peak shark-season southern weeks (June-November) and the marquee wreck routes fill earliest; hold a berth roughly 3-9 months out for peak windows and preferred vessels, with shoulder weeks bookable nearer term. Confirm current per-vessel lead times with the operator.

timing.peak: Apr-Jul (flamingo breeding, ~40,000 birds)
timing.notes: Río Lagartos flamingos peak Apr-Sep (breeding) — OPPOSITE window to Celestún (Nov-Mar). Follow-the-sun within Yucatán. Las Coloradas pinkest Mar + Jul-Aug. Sharpen on live tracking.

faq.q: When is the best time to see flamingos at Río Lagartos?
faq.a: April through July, the breeding concentration, when counts reach near 40,000 birds — the exact opposite window from Celestún, which peaks November–March. Counts swing year to year with water level and salinity, so book the reserve and the season, not a promised number, and sharpen on live tracking before committing to a date.

faq.q: Can you swim in the Las Coloradas pink lakes?
faq.a: Default no — plan for it. Las Coloradas is a working industrial hypersaline salt operation (Mexico's #2), not a swim beach; entry is rule-bound and guide-mandatory, and drones are banned by the salt company. A 2026 report suggests a limited, pre-booked 10-minute swim window may again be permitted at specific spots, but treat that as unconfirmed and volatile and default to the no-swim expectation.

faq.q: What else will I see besides flamingos?
faq.a: A full biosphere: 400+ logged bird species, crocodiles on the after-dark night run (mellow and family-friendly for older kids), the white halophilic-clay "Baño Maya" mud bath, and the salt-flat geology behind the pink. The reserve is a dedicated birding vertical once the Wildlife SI opens.

faq.q: Is there a beach at Río Lagartos?
faq.a: Yes — three quiet ones. Cancunito is a white-sand swim beach near town, San Felipe (12 km west) is a pastel fishing village with fresh seafood, and El Cuyo (45 min east) is a resort-free barrier-beach village inside the biosphere with steady side-shore wind for kitesurfing, peaking Dec–Feb.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Río Lagartos?
faq.a: Distance to trauma care, not crime. The town has only a basic clinic; Tizimín is ~1 hr, Valladolid's hospital ~1.5 hr (with 24-hr ambulance transfer for serious cases), and Mérida's full private hospitals ~2–2.5 hr. Serious injury means a long road transfer, so build the medevac distance into expectations, especially for older travelers, and carry insurance.

key_facts: Roatán sits on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the second-largest coral-reef system on earth; Bay Islands ranked highest in coral health in the 2015 Mesoamerican assessment.
30+ dive shops on the west side; ~30 named dive sites within a 10-minute boat ride off West Bay/West End, with walls dropping past 100 ft and the El Aguila/Odyssey wrecks.

Whale sharks are snorkel-only and protected; Utila (a short hop from Roatán) offers year-round potential peaking late March-April.
Roatán has an on-island recompression chamber (Cornerstone Hyperbaric, adjacent to Anthony's Key Resort; DAN IPPN partner) — a first-response advantage for wall diving.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: The load-bearing risk is mainland crime, and the plan is to stay in-zone. Violent crime and gang activity concentrate in the San Pedro Sula, Tegucigalpa, and Comayagua corridors, and Gracias a Dios Department carries a Level 4 "Do Not Travel" rating — all on the mainland. Fly direct into RTB, keep the trip airport → island, and never route overland through the gang zones.

faq.q: Is diving Roatán's walls dangerous — and can I fly out afterward?
faq.a: Wall diving rewards depth discipline and respect for the no-fly window, and Roatán has an unusual first-response advantage. Recreational divers work the crest and upper wall (≤60–100 ft); wreck and deep-wall profiles trend technical and are certification-gated. Allow no-fly-after-diving of 18–24 hours before your RTB flight, and note the on-island Cornerstone Hyperbaric Chamber (adjacent to Anthony's Key Resort, a DAN partner) — a genuine safety edge for a wall-diving island. **What makes Roatán's diving special? ** *(Dive Liveaboards / Diving)* Roatán delivers a serious wall reef within minutes of the dock plus a rare repeat-rate track record. Within a 10-minute boat ride off West Bay/West End you reach ~30 named dive sites, from a 15-ft sandy playground with feeding eagle rays to 100-ft+ wall drop-offs, wrecks, and canyon swim-throughs; CoCo View Resort claims the highest repeat rate of any dive resort worldwide (1,600+ guests five times over).

faq.q: How much is the Roatán reef fee, and is it required?
faq.a: Yes, it is mandatory and it is small. The Roatán Marine Park conservation fee is $10/year or $5/day, non-commissionable, and it funds the very reef you came to dive and snorkel — present it as the reef's cover charge, never buried.

faq.q: Is Roatán good for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes — Roatán runs a genuine adults-only luxury lane on top of the diving. Ibagari Boutique Hotel is adults-only (12+), holds a Michelin Key 2025, and sits between West Bay and West End; private West Bay villas and sunset-cocktail liveaboard finales round out the romance product.

faq.q: Can I snorkel with whale sharks from Roatán?
faq.a: Yes, via a day-trip to neighboring Utila, and only by snorkel. Utila is one of the few places on earth with year-round whale-shark potential, peaking late March–April; the animals are protected, so it is surface snorkeling only — no diving with them and no touching.

name: Ruaha National Park
line: One in ten of the world's lions, wild dogs

key_facts: Tanzania's largest national park (~20,226 km2) and a global lion stronghold - an estimated ~10% of the world's lions, in some of the largest prides ever recorded (hunt buffalo and even giraffe)

One of East Africa's best wild-dog destinations - within the 3rd-largest wild-dog population in the world; ~12,000 elephants in the greater ecosystem; a rare East-meets-Southern-Africa transition zone (greater + lesser kudu, sable, roan)
The Great Ruaha River is the dry-season lifeline and focus of game viewing; 570+ birds; remote, uncrowded, mainly fly-in (south-central Tanzania, ~130 km west of Iringa)
US L3 Reconsider Travel - terrorism concern is the Mtwara Region (far southeastern coast, well away); bookable with L3 disclosure + consent; disclose LGBTQ+ targeting; travel with a licensed operator

Best Jun-Oct (dry - game on the river); green season Nov-Apr lush/birdy (some camps close); Ruaha's signature is the walking safari (+ night drives + fly-camping); no rhino (poached out - four of Big Five)

Sold via Tanzanian safari DMCs + camp consortia 10-20%+ - IATAN/host-gated, CLIA has NO Africa representation; light-aircraft fly-in + TANAPA park fees are pass-through; TZS (~2,633/USD, USD is the safari currency); eVisa; AMREF evac essential (remote interior)

safety.hospital: Remote deep-interior - medical access by air; AMREF Flying Doctors (~$40 pp/30d) + travel-medical insurance essential; nearest referral Iringa/Dar
safety.yellow_fever: not required direct from US/Europe; mandatory if transiting >12h through a risk country (e.g. Kenya)
safety.activity_note: L3 DISCLOSE + CONSENT (terrorism concern is the far-southeastern Mtwara Region, well away; disclose LGBTQ+ targeting - same-sex relations criminalized; travel with a licensed operator). Ruaha is a remote fly-in wilderness - AMREF evac + insurance are load-bearing. Walking safari only with armed ranger (single file, downwind, no bright colors); predator-dense driving (keep still/quiet, never on foot near a kill); night drives to vehicle rules

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for at Ruaha?
faq.a: Not the parks - the advisory's concerns are the far-southeastern Mtwara Region (terrorism, far away) and city petty crime, plus a flagged LGBTQ+ targeting concern travelers should weigh (Tanzanian law criminalizes same-sex relations). In Ruaha itself the risks are ordinary safari ones plus remoteness - it's a fly-in wilderness, so carry AMREF evac + insurance and follow the walking-safari rules.

faq.q: Why choose Ruaha over the northern circuit?
faq.a: For wildness and predators without the crowds - ~10% of the world's lions in huge prides, one of the world's best wild-dog populations, big elephant herds and a transition-zone game roster, all in Tanzania's largest park with a fraction of the vehicles. It's the connoisseur's safari, best paired with Nyerere/Selous.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Ruaha?
faq.a: The dry season, Jun-Oct, when the Great Ruaha River becomes the only water and game - lions, dogs, elephants - concentrates dramatically along it; the green season (Nov-Apr) is lush and superb for birds (570+ species) but some camps close and roads soften.

faq.q: How do I get to Ruaha, and how long should I stay?
faq.a: Mostly by light-aircraft fly-in (from Dar, Iringa or as part of a southern-circuit hop); give it 3-4 nights to justify the flight and to do the river drives and a walking safari - it's not a day-trip park.

faq.q: Do I need a visa or yellow-fever certificate for Tanzania?
faq.a: eVisa required - apply on the official portal before departure. Yellow fever is not required direct from the US/Europe, but is mandatory if you transit >12 h through a risk country like Kenya.

faq.q: What is the Juayúa food festival?
faq.a: The Feria Gastronómica is the route's flagship weekend market: every Saturday and Sunday, 11am–5pm, free entry, cash only, with the plaza filling with grills and pots — grilled meats $6–9, seafood ~$7, soups $3–4, pupusas ~$0.60, and roughly $10–20 feeds one person across multiple dishes. *[Culinary]*

faq.q: Is Joya de Cerén worth visiting?
faq.a: Yes — it is El Salvador's only UNESCO World Heritage site, a 7th-century Maya farming village buried and preserved by volcanic ash, earning the name "Pompeii of the Americas." Open 9–4 and closed Mondays with an on-site museum, it pairs with the Tazumal ruins (~$5 entry, ~40 min away) into one Maya-heritage day. *[Culture & Heritage]*

faq.q: Is the Santa Ana volcano hike dangerous?
faq.a: It is managed, not casual. Santa Ana (Volcán Ilamatepec, 2,381 m) is an active, monitored volcano with a turquoise sulphur crater lake and volcanic gas near the rim; the ~4–5 hour summit hike is guided-only, at scheduled departure times, and is subject to closure on activity alerts. Do not attempt it unguided, and confirm open status before booking.

faq.q: What outdoor adventures are on the Ruta de las Flores?
faq.a: The GEA spine runs from Santa Ana's turquoise crater and Cerro Verde to Lake Coatepeque (a volcanic caldera lake beneath the volcano), plus Apaneca's cloud-forest canopy ziplines (Los Enganches ~420 m lines) and the Laguna Verde crater lake ~5 km from Apaneca. Waterfall hikes at Los Chorros / Siete Cascadas round it out. *[GEA]*

faq.q: Where do couples stay on the Ruta de las Flores?
faq.a: Two romance bookends: coffee-finca boutique on the route itself — Hotel Santa Leticia, a 19-room working-estate lodge from ~USD 78/night — or lakeside luxe on Lake Coatepeque, where Cardedeu Residence is a 5-star hotel and Equinoccio a boutique lakeside stay with balcony rooms over the water. There is no international five-star flag on the route. *[Romance]*

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: Guided-only adventure and mountain roads. The Siete Cascadas 7-waterfall hike (~6 hrs) requires a mandatory guide (~$15/person) because of flash-flood, slick-rock, and cliff-jump hazards; canopy ziplines are operator-run with harness and briefing. The route itself is a cobblestone-and-switchback mountain drive — go in daylight, watch for highland fog, and prefer a local driver at night.

name: Saas-Fee
line: The Pearl of the Alps

key_facts: Car-free village since 1951 (park at entrance; electric buggies only) — the 'Pearl of the Alps', Saas Valley, Valais, ~1,800 m
Ringed by thirteen 4,000-m peaks (Dom, Allalinhorn, Weissmies, Nadelhorn, Lenzspitze) — densest cluster in the Alps (official site markets 38 regional — flagged)

Ski area on the Feegletscher/Allalin glacier: ~100 km pistes (Wikipedia cites 150 km — flagged), ~20/60/20 easy/intermediate/difficult, ~22-23 lifts, base 1,800 m to ~3,500 m Mittelallalin (summit ~3,573 m)
Metro Alpin = highest underground funicular in the world (to Mittelallalin ~3,500 m); Allalin = highest revolving restaurant in the world
Glacier + SUMMER skiing on the Allalin (national-team summer training base); operating window ~mid-Jul to late Apr
Adult day pass ~CHF 83 (youth ~71 / child ~42, via skiresort.info — verify live + Metro Alpin surcharge); Magic Pass member; no Ikon/Epic
SaastalCard on arrival = free valley cable cars + PostBus (Metro Alpin excluded)
Car-free arrival: SBB rail to Visp (or Brig) + PostBus line 511 Visp->Saas-Fee every 30 min
Luxury base: The Capra Saas-Fee (boutique 5-star) + Ferienart Resort & Spa (ratings/spa detail to verify)
Haute Route glacier ski-touring runs from the Saas valleys; thirteen 4,000-m peaks give guided summer mountaineering from the village
Glacier descent ~1,773 m vertical from Mittelallalin (~3,500 m) to the village (~1,800 m); ~60% intermediate terrain = progression/family-friendly
Two-season rhythm: winter + spring skiing, summer break for lower runs, Allalin glacier reopens in high summer
Sits east of Zermatt in the same Valais high country — the quiet glacier village to Zermatt's Matterhorn headliner; pairs on one Valais itinerary
No natural hot springs in-village; Valais thermal baths at Leukerbad are a scenic down-valley day-trip

safety.emergency: 112 / 117 police / 118 fire / 144 ambulance / 1414 REGA alpine air-rescue / 145 poison
safety.hospital: Visp/Brig (Spital Visp / Oberwallis) down-valley; local village medical practice for day cases; REGA 1414 alpine/glacier evac
safety.activity_note: Glacier ski area — avalanche AND crevasse risk: SLF five-level bulletin (slf.ch/White Risk), transceiver/shovel/probe + qualified guide off-piste, glacier off-piste roped-and-guided only, altitude/AMS (Mittelallalin ~3,500 m), sudden whiteouts; car-free village = strong child-safety upside; rescue REGA 1414

name: Salzburg
line: Mozart's baroque jewel

key_facts: Historic Centre UNESCO 1996 (~1,000 buildings); node co-FLAGSHIP + Salzkammergut/Berchtesgaden base
Mozart's Birthplace (Getreidegasse 9); DomQuartier; Mozart Week (Jan)
Hohensalzburg = largest preserved fortress in Central Europe; 1892 Festungsbahn funicular
Sound of Music locations (Mirabell/Hellbrunn/Leopoldskron/Mondsee)

Salzburg Festival founded 1920 (Jedermann on Cathedral steps 22 Aug 1920; world's largest classical festival, 200+ performances/15 venues/80 countries) — 17 Jul-30 Aug 2026 (+ Whitsun 22-25 May); Christkindlmarkt roots to 1491, 1M+ visitors, 19 Nov 2026-1 Jan 2027
Hohensalzburg begun 1077, 250x150 m, never captured (only siege 1525 failed); present look ~1500 (Leonhard von Keutschach)
DomQuartier reunited Residenz+cathedral+St Peter's in 2014 (first time in ~200 yrs); Mirabell Palace 1606 + gardens from 1687 + Pegasus Fountain 1913 (Marble Hall wedding venue)
Hellbrunn built 1612-1615 (Markus Sittikus) — gravity-fed Renaissance trick fountains + Sound of Music gazebo; St. Peter Stiftskulinarium recorded AD 803 = oldest restaurant in Central Europe
Ski amadé 760 km piste / ~270 lifts / 25 areas ~50 km (30-60 min) south = baroque-city ski base; Untersberg cable car (1961) 456->1,776 m in 8.5 min
Salzburg-Berchtesgaden seam: Berchtesgaden in the Bavaria node, cross-link, no double-cover

name: Samburu National Reserve
line: Northern Kenya's wild frontier

key_facts: The 'Samburu Special Five' - Grevy's zebra (80%+ of the world's remaining), reticulated giraffe, Beisa oryx, gerenuk, Somali ostrich - arid-country species found ONLY in Kenya's northern reserves, not the southern parks
~900 elephants + some of Kenya's best leopard (riverine forest of the Ewaso Ng'iro River); far fewer vehicles than the south - the connoisseur's Kenya
The Born Free legacy - George + Joy Adamson raised Elsa the lioness here; home of the proud Samburu people (cousins of the Maasai)
US L2 overall BUT far-north border counties (Mandera, Wajir, Garissa; parts of Marsabit/Turkana) are US L4 Do Not Travel - Samburu is NOT among them (mainstream safari zone); ROUTE VIA FLY-IN
Best Jul-Sep + Jan-Feb (dry); 2-3 days ideal, pairs with Laikipia (rhino); sold via Kenya safari DMCs 10-25% - IATAN/host-gated, CLIA has NO Africa representation
KES (~129/USD) + M-Pesa but safari quoted USD; eTA required; malaria prophylaxis advised (chloroquine-resistant); YF only if arriving from a risk country; AMREF Flying Doctors for evac

safety.hospital: Remote north - AMREF Flying Doctors (~$40 pp/30d) + travel-medical insurance; nearest referral Nanyuki/Nairobi

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Samburu?
faq.a: The northern-frontier context and remoteness. Stick to the licensed-operator reserve programme (fly-in recommended over long northern road transfers), follow your guide with dangerous game, and carry AMREF Flying Doctors (~$40 pp/30 days) + travel-medical insurance - public EMS is limited in the north. Malaria prophylaxis is essential.

faq.q: What makes Samburu different from the Mara or Amboseli?
faq.a: The Special Five - Grevy's zebra, reticulated giraffe, oryx, gerenuk and Somali ostrich you won't see in the southern parks - plus top leopard in the riverine forest, elephants on the Ewaso Ng'iro, and far fewer vehicles. It's the connoisseur's Kenya.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Samburu?
faq.a: Jun-Sep and Jan-Feb (dry) - hot and dry, when wildlife concentrates on the river and game-viewing peaks (Jul-Sep is the sweet spot). The green rains bring lush scenery, birdlife and lower rates.

faq.q: How many days do I need in Samburu?
faq.a: 2-3 days is ideal to work the river circuits and find the Special Five plus leopard; it pairs naturally with Laikipia (rhino, an hour's drive/short hop) or the Mara/Amboseli.

faq.q: Do I need a visa or yellow-fever certificate for Kenya?
faq.a: An eTA (Kenya replaced visas with the eTA in 2024 - apply at least 2 weeks ahead). Yellow fever is compulsory only if you arrive from a YF-risk country; CDC recommends the vaccine for most.

name: San Andrés & Providencia, Colombia
line: Coral islet, seven-colour sea

key_facts: San Andrés — the 'Sea of Seven Colors' — is Colombia's Caribbean crown jewel, ringed by coral with 40+ mostly-shallow, high-visibility dive sites.
Providencia + Santa Catalina sit on the third-largest barrier reef in the world; Providencia rebuilt after Hurricane Iota (2020) and is open to tourism in 2026.
The Raizal are a Black Colombian Afro-Caribbean people; 20,000–30,000 speak San Andrés–Providencia Creole (Islander English) and most are trilingual.
Rondón — fish, conch, cassava, plantain and yam simmered in coconut milk — is the island's signature dish ('run down').
Mandatory Tourist Card (Tarjeta de Turismo) ~COP 153,000 (2026), bought at the airline counter before boarding the flight to ADZ.

faq.q: What are the best beaches and cays on San Andrés?
faq.a: Johnny Cay is the headline — a protected 4-ha coral islet ~1.5 km off San Andrés Town with the best white sand around, reached by colectivo boat — plus calm snorkel pools at La Piscinita and West View, and mellow Rocky Cay off San Luis. The lagoon is the famed "Sea of Seven Colors."

faq.q: Is San Andrés good for scuba diving?
faq.a: Yes — it's a shallow-water reef diver's dream, with 40+ dive sites mostly at ~10–12 m, high-visibility and beginner-friendly, run through island PADI centers like Banda and Sharky. Providencia adds wall diving on the third-largest barrier reef in the world. Note it's day-boat reef diving, not liveaboard-berth product.

faq.q: Is Providencia good for a quiet honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes — Providencia is the quiet-honeymoon jewel: near-empty coves, the McBean Lagoon marine park, and Crab Cay (its #1 snorkel spot, ~USD $6 park fee) reached by express boat. It's rebuilt and open after Hurricane Iota (2020); reach it by ~20-minute inter-island flight or catamaran.

faq.q: What language and culture will I find on San Andrés?
faq.a: A living Raizal Afro-Caribbean nation: 20,000–30,000 people speak San Andrés–Providencia Creole (Islander English) and most are trilingual, descended from 18th-century Jamaican settlers and enslaved Africans. The signature plate is rondón — fish, conch and root vegetables simmered in coconut milk.

faq.q: What's the real day-to-day risk on the island?
faq.a: Not the mainland headlines — the island's real risks are petty/beach theft, motorcycle snatch-and-grab, scooter accidents and sea/riptide hazards. Renting a scooter or golf cart is the classic island loop, and scooter crashes plus snatch-and-grab are the two most common tourist mishaps: helmet on, valuables off the seat, drive in daylight.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in San Blas?
faq.a: Remoteness, not crime. There is no hospital and, on most cays, no clinic; serious illness or injury means evacuation to Panama City or the US, which can exceed $50,000. Comprehensive travel + medevac insurance is a condition of going, not an option — and dengue/malaria risk is year-round.

faq.q: Are the boat crossings and the 4x4 access road dangerous?
faq.a: Manageable but weather-governed. Everything moves by open boat, so insist on worn life vests, a licensed captain, and a real forecast check; the Colombia passage is 24–52 hours at open sea with no turning back mid-crossing. The overland Cartí route is a steep, rain-sensitive mountain road needing a 4x4 (4–5 hours). Guided only.

faq.q: Which San Blas islands are best for beaches and snorkeling?
faq.a: The outer Cayos Holandeses (Dutch Cays) are widely rated the best snorkeling in the archipelago, with healthy reef and cushion starfish on the flats. Isla Perro holds the signature shallow-shipwreck snorkel a few metres from shore, while the Cayos Limones lagoon (Isla Pelícano, of *Money Heist* fame) offers the easiest crystal-shallow day-trip.

faq.q: Is San Blas good for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes, if you want elemental over polished. The set-piece is a private or near-private sand-cay cabaña — hammock, palm, reef at the doorstep, no wifi — from ~$56–$100/night full-board, scaling up to a private crewed catamaran overnight. Expect solar power and often no running water: this is the Caribbean before anyone built a lobby on it.

faq.q: What is the Panama-to-Cartagena sailing trip like?
faq.a: It's a genuine passage, not a lagoon cruise. Three days threading the San Blas cays, then 24–52 hours of open-water crossing to Colombia; shared cabins run ~$525–$750 (meals + immigration paperwork included), private from ~$900+. Small boats have limited cabins and sell out weeks ahead for dry-season departures.

faq.q: Who are the Guna, and how do I enter the comarca?
faq.a: You enter on Guna terms. The Guna are a matrilineal people who won semi-autonomy in the 1925 revolution and still govern by congress under saila leaders; entry means a passport check and a per-person cash fee (~$20/foreigner) at the Cartí checkpoint, with no ATMs on the islands. Buy reverse-appliqué molas direct from the women who sew them.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for — is the road dangerous?
faq.a: The connective road is the risk, not the city. Highway 199 between San Cristóbal and Palenque via Ocosingo has reported armed robberies (predominantly at night) plus periodic CNTE union blockades that usually cause only short delays. The rule is daytime-only overland travel with a vetted guide or private transfer, never a night self-drive; the city center itself is pedestrian-comfortable by day.

faq.q: What are San Juan Chamula and Zinacantán, and how do I visit respectfully?
faq.a: They are living Tzotzil Maya villages, 10 km out, and a guide is effectively mandatory. Chamula's church is a pine-needle-floored space of Maya-Catholic fusion with ritual healings day and night and a strict no-photography rule inside; Zinacantán (99% Indigenous) is a backstrap-loom weaving town with a women's co-op. Pay the community fees and follow a guide who knows the etiquette.

faq.q: What is there to do in the city itself?
faq.a: Walk the pedestrian andadores — Real de Guadalupe and the Andador Eclesiástico — between two hillside churches. The Templo de Santo Domingo has Chiapas's most elaborate carved pink facade with a Tzotzil/Tzeltal textile market at its churchyard, and the Museo del Ámbar (in the ex-convent of La Merced) shows amber with 25-million-year-old inclusions, alongside a strong Chiapas-coffee and cacao café culture.

faq.q: What is Sumidero Canyon, and is it worth it?
faq.a: Yes — it's the region's signature nature outing. A 2-hour open-boat cruise from the UNESCO colonial town of Chiapa de Corzo runs ~32 km beneath canyon walls up to ~1,000 m, past waterfalls and wildlife. It's a low-risk daytime trip with licensed operators — life vests on, weather-dependent.

faq.q: Is San Cristóbal a good base for a quiet, cultured couple's trip?
faq.a: Yes — it's cultured romance, not resort romance. At 2,200 m the highland evenings ask for a sweater; boutique colonial casas like Hotel Bö and Casa del Alma offer temazcal spa culture and courtyard dinners along cobblestone andadores. Come in the dry season (Nov–April), with crisp 18–24°C days, blue skies and minimal rain.

faq.q: Does the altitude affect visitors?
faq.a: Only mildly. At ~2,200 m some travelers feel light shortness of breath or a disturbed first night's sleep, but it is not a serious altitude risk — hydrate and ease into exertion on day one. Drink bottled water only; dengue is a lowland concern (Palenque, the canyon), not the cool highland city.

faq.q: What is the ATM cave tour like, and do you need a guide?
faq.a: It is the apex Cayo adventure and it is guided-only by law — you cannot legally enter Actun Tunichil Muknal without a licensed operator. Expect a ~45-minute jungle trek with multiple river crossings, a swim into the cave mouth, wading a shallow underground river in total darkness, and tight climbs; ~3 hours inside. Cameras have been banned since a 2012 incident cracked a ~1,000-year-old skull.

faq.q: How do you visit Caracol and Xunantunich?
faq.a: Differently. Caracol — whose Caana pyramid (141 ft/43 m) is Belize's tallest structure — requires a military-escorted convoy from the Douglas D'Silva Forest Station (muster ~9 am, return ~2 pm) because it sits near the porous Guatemala border. Xunantunich is easier: a 20-minute drive and a hand-cranked Mopan River ferry to El Castillo, ~40 m and the country's second-tallest structure.

faq.q: Is San Ignacio good for a honeymoon?
faq.a: Yes — for jungle romance rather than beach. The luxury lodge belt is world-class: Coppola's Blancaneaux Lodge (~20 rooms, Mountain Pine Ridge waterfalls), the 500-acre Green Globe reserve at Chaa Creek (founded 1981, with butterfly farm, spa and Macal River canoeing), and Ka'ana's plunge-pool villas. Plunge-pool casitas, canopy dinners and waterfall spas define the market.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for in Cayo?
faq.a: Water, wildlife and inland health, not urban crime. CDC advises avoiding swimming in fresh, unchlorinated water (leptospirosis), yet ATM and cave-tubing involve unavoidable river immersion, so treat them as guided-only informed-consent activities; high water after heavy rain periodically closes the caves. CDC also states malaria is a risk in some parts of Belize — treat the mainland jungle as potential risk and get a travel-medicine consult; dengue is present.

faq.q: Is the ATM cave tour dangerous?
faq.a: It is physically demanding but safe as a licensed, guided activity — there is no legal or safe self-tour option. The tour requires "good to very good" fitness for river fordings, swimming into the cave, and tight passages and climbs in the upper chambers, with a minimum height of ~40 inches. Cave-tubing and Barton Creek Cave are likewise licensed-guide-required, with rising-water hazard after rain.

faq.q: Is San José worth staying a night, or just an airport?
faq.a: Worth a night. It's the front door, not the destination — but the Pre-Columbian Gold Museum (~1,600 pieces, beside the Teatro Nacional), a three-museum pass (~$33), and the Barrio Escalante restaurant row give a genuine half-to-full day of culture-and-coffee substance.

faq.q: Can you day-trip Poás and Irazú volcanoes from San José?
faq.a: Yes — both are same-day from the capital. Irazú tops 3,432 m with both oceans visible on a clear morning; Poás runs a dynamic-access, online-only timed-entry model via SINAC, so go guided to absorb the timed-entry and closure logistics.

faq.q: Where is SJO airport and how busy does it get?
faq.a: Juan Santamaría (SJO) is Costa Rica's primary international gateway, 20 km northwest of downtown in Alajuela. It just set a record, handling 3,215,208 international passengers between Nov 2025 and Apr 5 2026 — up 7.9% year-over-year — so book gateway beds and transfers ahead of the dry-season wave.

faq.q: If something goes wrong in Costa Rica, is medical care nearby?
faq.a: Reassuringly, yes — San José IS the national medical and evacuation hub. Hospital Clínica Bíblica (founded 1929, JCI-accredited, 24/7, with an on-site heliport for evac) and the US-affiliated Hospital CIMA are both in the metro, so serious care and the evac hub are right here.

faq.q: Where's the top end for a honeymoon in San José?
faq.a: San José/Palmilla is the branded-ultra spine of Los Cabos: One&Only Palmilla (the 1956-origin icon, 27-hole golf), Zadún (a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, 115 villas), Chileno Bay and Esperanza (Auberge). It's the quiet, composed counterweight to Cabo San Lucas' nightlife.

faq.q: When can I see whales, and is the estuary worth it?
faq.a: Whale season is mid-December to mid-April with ~90–95% sightings at peak (mother-calf pairs Jan–Feb). For nature on land, the Estero de San José — BCS's only freshwater coastal lagoon and an Important Bird Area — holds 270+ bird species, best at dawn.

faq.q: Which San José beaches can I actually swim?
faq.a: Very few — most open Corridor beaches have strong currents and are not swim-safe. The reliable exception is Blue Flag Playa Palmilla, with a protected swimming area; Chileno and Santa María are the other Corridor swim beaches.

faq.q: What is the Art Walk, and when is it?
faq.a: Every Thursday evening, 5–9 pm, November through June, the Gallery District opens more than a dozen galleries along the cobblestone streets around Álvaro Obregón, with music and refreshments — and it's free. Book Art Walk-night dinner ahead Dec–March.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: The ocean and the weather, not crime. Most open San José beaches have dangerous rip currents — swim only at Blue Flag Palmilla or other designated coves — and hurricane season runs Jun–Nov, September historically worst. Carry trip insurance for green-season dates.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: The southern industrial corridor, plus altitude and cobblestones. The Level 3 driver is oil-theft ("huachicol") violence south along Hwy 45D — do not self-drive those routes. In town, the practical notes are a high-desert **~1,900 m** altitude (mild first-day effects) and steep cobblestone streets; Hospital MAC handles ER/ICU care, with advanced-trauma evac to Querétaro (~1 hr).

faq.q: Is SMA good for a destination wedding, and how far ahead do I book?
faq.a: Yes — it's Mexico's wedding capital, with a decades-deep planner/vendor ecosystem and venues for **20–300 guests**. The lead time is long: serious venue/planner inquiry runs **6–12 months** before the date, with the **Oct–Nov and Mar–May** weekends going first, so fire villa blocks a full engagement season ahead.

faq.q: What are the must-see culture sites?
faq.a: The pink Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel over the Jardín, the UNESCO historic center, the Fábrica La Aurora art complex, and — ~15 min north — the Santuario de Atotonilco (1740–1776), the "Sistine Chapel of the Americas," with six chapels of floor-to-ceiling baroque murals.

faq.q: What's the wellness scene?
faq.a: Thermal and ceremonial. La Gruta's hot springs run **37–40 °C**, reached through a ~20 m lit volcanic cave tunnel, and temazcal (pre-Hispanic sweat-lodge) ceremonies pair with hotel-spa culture like Belmond's Laja Spa — honeymoon-ready restoration.

faq.q: Is there a wine route?
faq.a: Yes — the under-the-radar Guanajuato wine route an hour from town, anchored by Cuna de Tierra (the state's oldest winery) and Viñedos San Miguel, and paired with Dolores Hidalgo's independence history and famous *nieves exóticas* (exotic ice creams).

faq.q: Can I book a stay in San Sebastián del Oeste?
faq.a: No — it is content-only, recommended only as a licensed day-trip from the Puerto Vallarta carve-out. Jalisco is US State Dept Level 3 (May 29, 2026), San Sebastián is not one of the four named carve-outs, and the advisory does not mention the town at all — so book_enabled=FALSE.

faq.q: What's the real risk to plan for?
faq.a: The mountain road transfer, not the town. The ~65 km / 1.5–2 hr drive on Hwy 544 leaves the PV safe zone through non-carve-out Sierra — the hold reason — and fog on narrow roads makes daytime, licensed transport essential. The nearest trauma hospital is ~1.5–2 hr back down in Puerto Vallarta.

faq.q: What is there to see in the colonial town?
faq.a: A 17th-century time capsule. Settled in 1605 for gold, San Sebastián keeps a near-intact 18th-century plaza and church, a mining museum, and the Mina Santa Gertrudis (~60 m mine cave); it is quiet and cool at ~1,480 m. Clearest touring is November–May.

faq.q: What's the coffee-and-raicilla scene like?
faq.a: It is the town's signature taste. The Sierra grows organic *café de altura* — La Quinta Mary is a 19th-century estate offering artisanal-process tours, and Hacienda Jalisco grows, processes and roasts its own — and San Sebastián is Mexico's #2 raicilla producer, a craft spirit distinct from tequila.

faq.q: What's the hiking like at Cerro de la Bufa?
faq.a: Short but remote. Cerro de la Bufa offers a viewpoint and summit trail with a panorama over Banderas Bay — the coast you left, seen from ~1,480 m and higher; go guided, start early on a clear dry-season morning, and turn back in fog, since trauma care is 1.5–2 hr away in PV.

faq.q: Can you do a wine tour from Santiago?
faq.a: Yes — the Maipo Valley, Chile's oldest and most decorated Cabernet appellation, is a 30-to-60-minute drive from the city, with icons like Concha y Toro (Pirque) and Almaviva (the 1997 Rothschild × Concha y Toro joint venture). Iconic winery tours book weeks-to-months ahead in high season, so reserve early.

faq.q: What are the top things to do in Santiago?
faq.a: Start high: Sky Costanera's 360° deck sits at 300 m on floors 61–62 of South America's tallest building, and Cerro San Cristóbal rises ~880 m inside the 722-hectare Parque Metropolitano to a 14-m Virgin visible citywide. Add Neruda's La Chascona, Lastarria dining, and the Mercado Central seafood halls.

faq.q: Is Santiago a good base for a romantic or luxe stay?
faq.a: Yes — the city carries a real luxe hotel bench with built-in romance. The Singular (Leading Hotels of the World), the Mandarin Oriental (the group's first South American property), and the 196-room W anchor Andes-view rooftops and wine-estate lunches; Viña Vik's 22 designer suites sit about two hours south.

faq.q: Can you ski from Santiago?
faq.a: Yes, in austral winter. Valle Nevado — the largest ski resort in the Southern Hemisphere at 3,000 m — is about 60 km / 1.5 hours from the city, a true day-trip from a hotel. Iconic Portillo, two hours out, runs its 2026 season June 20 → September 26.

faq.q: What's the real day-to-day risk in Santiago?
faq.a: Theft, not wilderness. The everyday risk is muggings, pickpocketing, and distraction/phone-snatch theft in crowded plazas, the metro, and markets, plus occasional protest cycles that can disrupt transit. Keep phones away in crowds, use vetted taxis or ride-hailing over street hails, and avoid demonstrations. Emergency numbers are 131 ambulance and 133 police.

faq.q: Is the altitude on the ski and canyon day-trips a problem?
faq.a: It can be for sensitive travelers. Embalse el Yeso sits at ~2,500 m and Valle Nevado at 3,000 m, so day-trippers gain real altitude within hours of sea-level Santiago — flag mild-AMS risk, hydrate, and acclimatize. On-piste skiing is resort-operated with patrol; backcountry and off-piste avalanche terrain are guided-only.

name: Saxon Switzerland
line: Germany's stone wilderness

key_facts: Germany's only rock national park, in the Elbe Sandstone Mountains (~700 km2, rock ~100 million years old)
The Bastei = pinnacles ~190 m above the Elbe + Bastei Bridge (wooden 1824, stone 1851) + ruined Neurathen rock castle
Koenigstein Fortress = one of Europe's largest hilltop fortresses; 9.5-ha plateau 240 m above the Elbe, never conquered, ~600k visitors/yr (adult ~EUR 6)
Malerweg (Painters' Way) ~116 km / 8 stages (opened 2006); follows Zingg + Graff (1766) and Caspar David Friedrich
Felsenbuehne Rathen ~1,800-seat rock stage, open-air since 1936; Saxon State Theatres May-Sep
Kirnitzschtalbahn narrow-gauge tram since 1898 (~8 km, Bad Schandau-Lichtenhain); Schrammsteine ridge + Lilienstein table mountain
Saxon climbing ~1,100 towers + ~17,000 routes; first ascent Falkenstein 1864; Saxon Climbing Rules (Fehrmann 1913): free climbing only, no metal, no chalk
Dresden = gateway (~45 min, own dossier); Czech side = Bohemian Switzerland cross-link; LOW-mountain sandstone, NOT alpine (no avalanche)
